claim: For every finite set D of distinct integers d >= 3 with gcd(D) = 1 and sum_{d in D} 1/(d-1) >= 1, and every integer k >= 1, there exists N(D,k) such that every integer n >= N(D,k) is a sum of finitely many labelled occurrences d^j with d in D and j >= k, each pair (d,j) used at most once; equal numerical values from different pairs remain separately available.

quadruple.statement: Candidate C1, not established: for every admissible D and k in claim, and every finite set F of deleted labelled occurrences, list the remaining occurrences in nondecreasing numerical order as a_1,a_2,..., breaking ties by base label, and put S_m=sum_{i=1}^m a_i; there exist integers L >= 0 and m_0 >= 1 such that every integer in [L,S_m-L] is a subset sum of the first m occurrences for every m >= m_0.
quadruple.stage: Labelled finite subset sums of integer geometric streams, ordered by numerical value with repeated occurrences retained.

shape.objects: Finite sets D of natural numbers, infinite locally finite labelled streams (d,j), and finite selected exponent subsets; each representation is reached by appending unused occurrences to a finite prefix. Finset, Nat powers and finite sums are definable in Lean/Mathlib.
shape.quantifiers: For every admissible finite D, for every integer k >= 1, there exists an integer N, for every integer n >= N, there exist finite subsets S_d of {k,k+1,...} such that n = sum_{d in D} sum_{j in S_d} d^j.
shape.target_quantity: A yes/no eventual-coverage decision; an unspecified threshold N(D,k) suffices, and no explicit numerical optimum is requested.
shape.ambient_structure: Integer order and modular arithmetic coexist. Adding an unused occurrence replaces a finite subset-sum set T by T union (T+a), preserving occurrence uniqueness. This recursion propagates a represented interval when its length is at least the next occurrence.
shape.symmetries: Permutations of base labels and complement symmetry in any finite prefix preserve subset-sum feasibility; adding bases helps, whereas a common dilation changes the represented lattice. Arbitrary translation or rescaling is not a symmetry of the original streams.
shape.configuration: The additive relation n=sum d^j requires coefficients in {0,1} for each labelled pair and eventual integer coverage. Deleting low powers destroys the zero-cutoff initial interval, and deleting a base may destroy the reciprocal or gcd hypothesis.
shape.extremal_candidate: No extremal counterexample is known. Equality families {3,4,7}, {3,5,7,13}, and {3,6,7,13,21} have published cutoff-1 completeness; none is treated as a counterexample.
shape.finite_certificates: Individual n representability has an explicit finite witness, and each fixed bounded instance can be checked. Neither the full all-D all-k assertion nor infinitely many omissions has a known complete finite reduction. Any seed interval must be paired with a proved infinite extension bound.
shape.monotonicity: Coverage is monotone when bases are added or cutoff is decreased. The general smallest positive cutoff k=1 remains open; fixed-D results with cutoff-dependent enlargements of D do not give all k.
shape.uniformity_parameter: All positive cutoffs for each fixed admissible finite D, including reciprocal equality; no common effective N over all D is requested.
shape.proof_shape: The full statement has explicit quantifiers in Erdos124.erdos124.ne_zero. The known zero-cutoff proof is Brown interval induction beginning with 1. The natural positive-cutoff induction lacks a seed interval; scalar prefix-capacity estimates and modular residue coverage are documented tools, but do not yet yield an all-D all-k proof. Disjoint sumset supplies in Bergelson-Simmons avoid reusing occurrences. No finite tail reduction or complete lemma chain for the root is established.
shape.neighbours: Known true: zero-cutoff Brown completeness as a combinatorial interval principle; bounded-gap finite sums under bounded prefix deficit (BEGL96 and Bergelson-Simmons); finite residue coverage from tail gcd; strong completeness under the disjoint-block hypotheses of Bergelson-Simmons Theorem 1.23. Known false: finite deletion preserves completeness for arbitrary sequences (powers of 2 lose odd sums). Open in inspected sources: the full positive-cutoff conjecture. Modified abstract sequences with bounded-gap finite sums can fail completeness, as Bergelson-Simmons Examples 1.7-1.8 show. No proved category equivalence or unchanged continuous model of the integer claim is recorded.
shape.known_bounds: BEGL96 p.137 supplies cutoff-1 exceptions 581,111,16,78 for the four listed families. Zero-cutoff induction has the initial-1 ceiling after deletion; scalar bounded-deficit estimates give syndeticity rather than cofiniteness, as Bergelson-Simmons explicitly distinguish. Their Theorem 1.23 uses three disjoint mass-at-least-one blocks and a separate gcd-one block. No bounded counterexample domain, finite root residue, divergent first-moment bound, or independent uniform constant settling the target is recorded.
shape.base_theory: Classical number theory in ZFC, with finite and countable objects only; no independence or extra set-theoretic axiom is known or proposed. Elementary finite verification and the intended proofs lie within Lean's standard classical axioms when formalized.

known: Aristotle/Alexeev: all nonnegative n at cutoff 0 by Brown induction; https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.24.0/ErdosProblems/Erdos124b.lean.
BEGL96: positive-density infinite bases yield cutoff-dependent finite complete subsets; cutoff-1 examples and interval-base estimates on p.137; DOI 10.4064/aa-77-2-133-138.

Bergelson-Simmons: bounded prefix deficit implies syndetic finite sums, and Theorem 1.23 gives strong completeness with three disjoint reciprocal blocks and a gcd-one supply; arXiv:1507.02208v2, DOI 10.4064/aa8221-10-2016.
